qs.q: Sibling nodes may exist for every node in the tree data structure except the ..... node.
e: Siblings are nodes that have the same parent.
Every node except the root has exactly one parent, so only the root has no siblings.
Leaves and internal nodes can have siblings.

qs.q: In a complete balanced binary tree with 10 nodes, how many levels are there?
e: A complete binary tree fills every level completely except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right.
Level 0 holds 1 node, level 1 holds 2, level 2 holds 4: total 7 nodes.
The remaining 3 nodes go to level 3, so the levels are 0, 1, 2, 3 = 4 levels.
Check with the formula: minimum height = $\lceil \log_2(10+1) \rceil - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3$ (height counted in edges), i.e. 4 levels.

qs.q: ..... trees are characterized by the concentration of their nodes on either side of the root.
e: In a skewed (degenerate) tree each node has only one child, so all nodes pile up on one side of the root.
Such a tree is unbalanced: its height grows like a linked list instead of staying close to $\log n$.
Balanced and complete trees spread the nodes across both sides.

qs.q:
What is the post-order traversal sequence corresponding to the tree shown in Figure (c)?
```
A has children B (left) and C (right)
B has children D (left) and E (right)
C has children F (left) and G (right)
D has children H (left) and I (right)
E has a left child J
J has a right child L
G has a left child K
```

c.x: H D I B J L E A F C K G
A B D H I E J L C F G K
H I D L J E B F K G C A
K G F C L J E I H D B A

e: Post-order rule: Left, Right, Root (the root is visited last).
Left subtree of A (root B): D's subtree gives H I D; E's subtree gives L J E (L, then J, then E); then B. So: H I D L J E B.
Right subtree of A (root C): F, then G's subtree K G, then C. So: F K G C.
Finally the root A. Full sequence: H I D L J E B F K G C A.
Option 1 is the in-order traversal, option 2 is the pre-order traversal, and option 4 is the reverse of the level structure, not a post-order.

qs.q: Which of the following observations regarding binary tree traversals is incorrect?

c.x: Given a pre-order traversal of a binary tree, the root node is the first occurring item in the list.
Given a post-order traversal of a binary tree, the root node is the last occurring item in the list.
In-order traversal does not directly reveal the root node of the binary tree.
It is necessary to have in-order, post-order, and pre-order traversal sequences in order to trace the binary tree's structure.

e: Pre-order is Root, Left, Right, so the root is the first item: statement 1 is correct.
Post-order is Left, Right, Root, so the root is the last item: statement 2 is correct.
In-order is Left, Root, Right, so the root is somewhere in the middle and cannot be spotted directly: statement 3 is correct.
Statement 4 is incorrect: all three sequences are not needed. An in-order sequence together with a pre-order or post-order sequence is enough to determine the tree.

qs.q: The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height k is
e: With the root at level 0, level L has at most $2^L$ nodes.
Summing the levels 0 to k gives $2^0 + 2^1 + \dots + 2^k = 2^{k+1} - 1$.
Example: height 2 gives $2^3 - 1 = 7$ nodes (a perfect tree with 1 + 2 + 4 nodes).

qs.q: True or False: A tree node's degree is equal to the number of its subtrees.
e: The degree of a node is the number of children it has.
Each child is the root of one subtree, so the number of children equals the number of subtrees.
Example: in a tree where A has children B and C, Degree(A) = 2.

qs.q: True or False: The maximum number of nodes on level i of a binary tree is $2 \times 2^{i-1}$, for $i \ge 1$.
e: The range $i \ge 1$ means the root is counted as level 1 (the second convention mentioned in the lecture).
Each level has at most twice the nodes of the previous one: level 1 has 1 node, level 2 has 2, level 3 has 4, so level i has at most $2^{i-1}$.
The statement gives $2 \times 2^{i-1} = 2^i$, which is twice too large (for example 2 nodes at the root level), so it is False. (With the root at level 0, the lecture's formula is $2^L$.)

qs.q: True or False: A binary tree of height h is considered to be complete only when the maximum number of nodes ($2^h - 1$) is preserved.
e: A complete binary tree only requires every level to be full except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right.
Having the maximum number of nodes means every level is full: this is a perfect binary tree, which is a special case of a complete tree.
So a complete tree does not need the maximum number of nodes, and the statement is False.

qs.q: True or False: The depth of a node is the distance between the root and the node in question.
e: The level (depth) of a node indicates its distance from the root, measured as the number of edges on the path from the root.
Example: the root is at level 0, its children at level 1, and their children at level 2.

qs.q: In a/an ____ traversal, we traverse the left sub-tree first, then we traverse the right sub-tree, and finally we visit the root.
e: Post-order is Left, Right, Root: the root comes after its children.
Pre-order is Root, Left, Right; in-order is Left, Root, Right; level-order visits level by level using a queue.

qs.q: Tree ____ is a used pattern to visit all the nodes in the tree.
e: Tree traversal means visiting every node of the tree in a particular order (preorder, inorder, postorder, level-order).
Search, insertion and deletion deal with one specific node and do not visit all nodes.

qs.q: If each node in the tree has a maximum of two children, we say the tree is a/an ____ tree.
e: A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most two children, normally called the left child and the right child.
Ternary would allow three children and unary only one.

qs.q: In a tree structure, the level of a node n is the number of ____ on the path from the root node to n.
e: The level of a node is its distance from the root, i.e. the number of edges on the path from the root to it (root at level 0).
Example: for the path A to C to F the path length is 2 edges, so F is at level 2.

qs.q: Which traversal visits nodes in the order: Left, Root, Right?
e: In-order: Left, Root, Right (the root comes in between its children).
Pre-order is Root, Left, Right and post-order is Left, Right, Root.
Example: for the tree A (children B, C; B has D, E; C has F, G) the in-order is D B E A F C G.

qs.q: Which traversal visits the nodes in the order: Root, Left, Right?
e: Pre-order visits the root before its children: Root, Left, Right.
Example: for the tree A (children B, C; B has D, E; C has F, G) the pre-order is A B D E C F G.
Level-order visits level by level with a queue instead.

qs.q: A node in a tree with no children is called a:
e: A leaf (external) node is a node that has no children.
The root is the topmost node, and a parent is any node that has at least one child.

qs.q: In In-order traversal of a Binary Search Tree, the output is always:
e: In a BST, smaller values are in the left subtree and greater values in the right subtree.
In-order visits Left, Root, Right, so values come out in increasing order.
Example: the BST with root 50 (30, 70; 20, 40, 60, 80) gives 20 30 40 50 60 70 80.

qs.q: A Binary Search Tree property ensures that for any node:
e: BST ordering rule: values smaller than a node go into its left subtree and values greater go into its right subtree.
So for any node: left < node < right. Option 1 states only half of the rule.
The root is not the smallest (it is between left and right values), and nodes are not all equal.
